utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I was informed that you would like to address the Chamber for less than a minute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning. The reason why we want to intervene this morning is the following, it is of a public character, it's to do with the agenda organisation, it is absolutely necessary for the Defence to know how the organisation of the schedule will continue so that we can present our case until its very end. I think it is the right of the Defence to know whether, yes or no, the Prosecution is going to continue with the rebuttal or not and to give us clear answers because all of us, I believe, should be able to organise ourselves and in order to do this, we have to know what's happening and I think the time has come now for the Prosecution to stop not giving us information and to speak up openly about this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I think the Rules cover the issue of the rebuttal case and we'll comply with the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the directions of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider the matter during a meeting in Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During a meeting in Chambers, there has been some discussion as to what information should be given. The Prosecution has taken the view that at the end of the presentation of the Defence case, that they would have to announce or whether they would like to present any evidence in rebuttal and they also have indicated that perhaps and they at that time mentioned one issue that they perhaps might be willing to give some information prior to that very moment. The Chamber has considered the matter and as it stands now, it could be expected that at least a couple of days will be needed for the Prosecution, if they apply for leave to present rebuttal evidence would be needed and then the same would be true for the Defence so that some time will be given to prepare for that but that would be not more than just a couple of days, certainly not more than three, four, five days. As far as -- I do understand that the Defence takes the view that the Prosecution is under an obligation now to announce what subjects they would like to cover during their rebuttal evidence; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that, but simply if, yes or no, the Prosecution wishes to do this. If I am allowing myself to make this intervention it's for a simple reason is that the counsel of the Defence, as well as the Prosecution counsel, are all independent people and they have their obligations outside of this courtroom. Personally, I have been asked to assent to the post of presidency in Switzerland and may I know whether the time will allow me to accept such a function or not and I think that here, law should be applied but also its a question of elementary courtesy as well as professional one, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I listened to the English channel and so therefore it's not clear from the transcript, perhaps you could repeat it what you have been asked to do in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have been asked to assent to a Presidency, Mr. President, and I have to know whether I will have time to devote myself to such and such a case or will be here for a number of weeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the -- as we can see now, after the Defence has finished the presentation of its case, it's in -- if the Prosecution wants to present rebuttal evidence, and I think it's clear that some rebuttal evidence in any case will be short to be presented, that would mean presumably that we would have a break of a couple of days then rebuttal evidence will be presented, then we might have another break of a couple of days in order to give the Defence an opportunity to indicate whether they want to present any further evidence but apart from two times a break of anything between three and five days, I think we could not expect to be out of this court for any longer and that would, as far as we can see it now, but of course a lot also depends on the parties and the speed they develop when examining witnesses, when presenting evidence, that I would say somewhere late March would be the final conclusion of the trial and I have then not yet included -- or perhaps -- but perhaps we -- it's better to sit together with the legal officer who is specifically at this moment that's Ms. Tournaye who is specifically dealing with scheduling the time we have given it quite some thought but as far as I can see, there will be only two times perhaps of a couple of days that we are not sitting in court up, up to five days. So if the parties would meet with Ms. Tournaye then they can get better information as to what the Chamber expects to happen but the course it's not the Chamber but it's mainly the parties who are -- I wouldn't say in control but are decisive factors in what will happen. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On a related issue, perhaps, is what time, if any, will be permitted the parties between the close of evidence and the filing of the closing briefs and the making of the final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would be helpful to the Prosecution at the least to have some indication of what time the Trial Chamber is contemplating, what period of time in that regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be relatively short because a lot can be prepared already prior to that very moment and -- but also that we do not know what the parties exactly would like to have -- how much time they would need, how much time they would claim to prepare for that, but perhaps this would be very good to deal with in a meeting with Ms. Tournaye and then of course finally the Chamber will decide. Yes. If there's nothing else at this moment to be dealt with urgently, I'd like to ask Mr. Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Vilicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I understand that you will resume the examination of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Before we talk about the Markale incident, I'd like to go back to some of the answers that you gave yesterday at the time of your examination yesterday. Yesterday, you said that when a primary charge was fired, in effect it is always -- the weapon was always charged with what we call the primary as well as the one increment charge; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: No, no, I couldn't have said that. I didn't say that. In fact, the fuse is part of the shell. The only thing that can be done on the fuse before the firing is it can be set to a time delay, if that is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible, if this is this type of the time-delay fuse. If you have the kind of fuse which can either be an instant-contact fuse or a time-delay fuse, the primary charge is in the stabiliser of the mine and the increment, first increment charge is supposed to go around the body of the stabiliser of the shell. And such a shell is then dropped down the barrel in an 82 millimetre mortar and then when the shell hits the firing pin, then the mortar is fired. There is a mechanism for firing so after the shell is dropped, you can then do another mechanism and then you can fire it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, what you said yesterday on the transcript that I'm quoting now, is the following, and this is where I would like some clarification, page 20.179 -- no, I'm sorry -- 20.179. Yesterday you said the following, and I'm going to quote now, line 4, [In English] "For 120 millimetre shell we have to use the primary plus one additional charge." [Interpretation] I don't know this is what you wanted to express yesterday, Professor, or whether you wanted to say that when it's a primary with one additional charge, that you are saying something that could be linked to another technical point. Could you please give us some clarifications? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As we know, a problem in interpretation, basic charge is the primary charge and the additional charge is the additional charge which is around the body of the stabiliser. You can have six increment charges, one to six depending how many are placed before the mortar is fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm going to come back to the transcript now. So is it possible, and I'm here speaking about all types of mortars, also the small mortar which is 60 or 62 millimetre calibre, and 82 millimetre calibre, 120 or even 81 millimetre calibre that we have occasionally, for these mortars, is it possible for them to be fired only with the primary charge, the basic charge? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I have to correct something. There is no 62 millimetre calibre mortar, there is 50, 60, 81 or 82, 120 and even a higher 140, 160 that are rare. Another thing, from all the mortars apart from the 120 millimetre mortar, it is possible to fire only with a primary charge, with a basic charge. In 120 millimetre calibre mortar, the basic charge, the primary charge does not make it possible to have sufficient speed to arm the fuse and that's why it is necessary to have the primary plus one or the first increment. In this case, the increment, the first increment is only used to arm, to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you, Professor. Then on page 30, I'm referring to the references from yesterday, the pagination of yesterday, you mentioned that it was perfectly possible to use a mortar to destroy troops and material like facilities that you mentioned for instance shelters, basements and so on. And you also mentioned a machine-gun nest as being one theoretical potential target perfectly compatible with the use of mortars. My question is the following: On this level, is there a difference between a machine-gun nest, whether it is high or on the ground level, and a sniper nest, if we can use this term?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I said that for machine-gun nest destruction, this is primarily to do with machine-gun nests that are located in bunkers on ground levels so more or less this is semi-open or open machine-gun nest, it's a machine-gun nest which is covered with timber, wood, and soil or with some other protective material. A mortar cannot be used to target a machine-gun nest if it is in a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, if now I have the following situation, this is a hypothetical question: A roof which would allow, either because it's open or because it's flat, to place a machine-gun nest on the top of the building, that is on the roof. In this hypothesis, could a mortar be something that could be used to reduce this, to eliminate this firing point, in fact, yes, to eliminate it? Yes or no, is it possible?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, if the machine-gun nest is located on the roof, and even if it's on the roof which is covered with tiles, roof tiles, the fact is that the mortar can go through the roof or if it's a flat roof as most tall buildings have flat roofs then you have use the mortar and you have can have the desired effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be feasible to attempt, and this is a purely theoretical question, to attempt to attack these surfaces either the higher storeys or these roofs that would have been covered by using mortars in order to try to cause damage to the lower floors by shelling the roof, would one damage the lower storeys? Would this method of attrition be feasible?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, only -- it depends on the construction of the building. If you used 120 millimetre shell which had delayed action, it could penetrate the roof providing it did that, the shell would penetrate down below and it would cause damage, but given the way shells are usually -- mortars are usually used -- well, there are other means that could be used to accomplish such a task. Hand-held anti-mortar devices are far more efficient, they penetrate far more walls. Usually up to about 1 metre they have an effect and more or less destroy everything that is in the area that they hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'd like to return to this matter. I think that you spoke about arms, weapons that could be used by just one man. I think you mentioned hand-held grenades, could you provide us with some more information about this kind of weapon, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can, since I worked on the development of such devices, I tested them, I have quite a lot of experience. These weapons are used for combatting anti-armour vehicles, among the weapons of the JNA. There are two types of such anti-armour weapons, those the old RBN 57 hand-held launcher and then for -- there was a rocket weapon with a cumulative warhead, a Zolja, a hand-held rocket launcher and we also had an anti-armour weapon with a retractive projectile. It was called an Osa. They could penetrate armour that was 300 millimetres thick and the primary purpose was to destroy armoured devices. They could also target bunkers which had walls which were up to 1 metre thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I'll stop you there. You're not the first to do this, but please try to slow down a bit for the sake of comprehension. For example, you mentioned a Zolja and then apparently something else but it wasn't caught by the court reporters. Could you tell us what the second device was?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: It's also an anti-armour weapon, the calibre of this weapon is 90 millimetres for multiple use. It's a launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What's its name?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Osa, O-s-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And was there something else before you mentioned the Osa?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: A Zolja, z-o-l-j-a. A Zolja and an Osa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's very clear now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Zolja is a 73 millimetre weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you know and do you have any information about this? Do you know whether these two weapons that you have mentioned were weapons that were generally part of the former JNA arsenal and did they have such weapons in their store houses?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes. These weapons were built and produced in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: And we produced large amounts of these weapons especially of Zoljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, since you were involved in the design and the production, I think, of these weapons, do you know whether these weapons could also have been intended for what we call the Territorial Defence arsenals?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you, teams involved in constructing weapons, so you shouldn't think that I was the person who constructed it. I know the names of the main constructers, the leaders of the teams, I can mention them: Mr. Lazarevic was involved in the Zolja; Mr. Jovanovic was involved with the Osas. They are the main constructers, but teams were involved in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the production process. These weapons and especially the Zolja, which were -- and large amounts of these weapons were produced, especially the Zolja, they were part of the main infantry units, part of their weapons and they were intended for the use of the Territorial Defence. So they were in warehouses where they kept weapons for Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm certain I have no doubts that such efforts are team efforts, but thank you for drawing our attention to this fact. But since you have had experience in teams and you know for whom these weapons were intended within Yugoslavia, I would like you to tell us, very briefly, because perhaps you have knowledge about this too, how were the warehouses organised, that is to say, the arsenals of the Territorial Defence? If you don't know anything about this, I'll move on to a different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stamp. The translators cannot translate your words unless the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as I have withdrawn my question and in any case, the Prosecution has been reduced to silence, there are no more problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question has been withdrawn as far as I understand, Mr. Stamp. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday it was on page 35 you told us that the precision of a shot could be affected by certain factors, namely the age of the ammunition used and the loss of weight, if I have understood this correctly. The loss of weight is problematic for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could be reminded of the part of the transcript where --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it was on page 35, but obviously I don't have the page today. It's page 35, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you mention a problem that had to do with weight, Professor, do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, we seem to have microphone problems at this very moment. When the red light is on, the microphone is on. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's how it was translated, that was an error. I didn't say anything like that. I said that dispersal is the result of a change in the powder charge. When the powder becomes old, it loses some of its characteristics so the speed at which it burns is changed. I won't go into all the details because of this, the pressure diminishes and the initial speed of the projectile changes and I said that a result of dispersal and it had to do with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat that part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you? The translators could not catch all of your answers and meanwhile, I could inform the parties that on my LiveNote it seems that we are talking about the testimony which appears on page 20.186 on from line 13 where the witness said something about the year of manufacture, the year of the charge being filled and the outside temperature, that's where I take it you were referring to, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With respect to fragmentation, not the position of shot which is the question Mr. Piletta-Zanin led the witness with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if I'm wrong, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that's where I find the word gunpowder and where the year of manufacture seems to be of importance. It seems to relate, rather, to the explosive --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's possible that I noted something last night but the Professor has provided elements of his answer that interest us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question is as follows: I'm talking about the shot now Professor, apart from the factors that you mentioned, the factors that you mentioned, are there any other factors that might influence the quality of a shot and I'm referring to the precision of a shot, other factors that would be exterior to the ammunition itself, if you know anything about this, which factors would they be?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I mentioned what the internal factors were, as you called them, factors which influence precision. They have to do with the projectile, the weapon, the sites, the system itself. We call that the weapons system. Precision, is in fact dispersion, not fragmentation, it has to do with the dispersion of the projectile and this is a function of a system deviation. I've already mentioned this, but the precision is influenced by how well the distance of the target is determined. If the distance is not set correctly, then the wrong information is used, and apart from the factors that I have mentioned, the system factors, the target man or the commander who is in charge of the weapon can introduce an external error, as you called it. So it can go too far or not far enough not just because of a system deviation but because of the mistakes introduced by the commander or the person targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that the shot could go very high and would then obviously fall. In the course of its trajectory, can the projectile encounter various weather conditions that might also cause deviations of the order that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, I mentioned weather conditions, so-called ballistics weather conditions and if you are not familiar with them, this can result in serious errors especially with mortars because mortar shells have curved trajectories. The projectile goes very high and this happens especially in conditions where you have so-called inversion. In the upper echelons, you have wind and in such cases, the range can be extended or shortened for the values by the values that have been given in the firing tables. They can be a fire deviation which amounts to ten seconds, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, yesterday, you showed us a table, we mentioned the existence of a table where you said in percentages what the chance of success or failure was in order to hit a target and this depended on the number of charges and the distance desired and the type of calibre used, the percentages such as 25 per cent, et cetera. My question now is as follows: These margins of error, if we should translate them not into percentages but into metres, what would that correspond to on the basis of your experience; that is to say, would the margin of error be about 10 metres or perhaps far more or far less?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The deviation, the distance deviation has to do with the dispersion and it's given in the firing tables. That magnitude depends on the range for one weapon system. The distance, the dispersion in distance increases when the range is greater. In the firing table for mortars you can see that it goes up to about 50 metres, that is one possible dispersion, and the statistical range in which you can find the greatest number of projectiles fired out in a series is four, five, VDs. So at a range of 6.000 metres, 120 millimetre mortar they can fall within a range of 200 and 250 metres, four to five VDs in the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please explain exactly what you mean by VDs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A VD is the possible margin of error which is determined for each system, for each projectile system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I'm afraid that I have to ask you to be a little clearer, for me at least. Let's imagine we have a target, a target A, and that I want to hit it with a mortar shell. Let's say that it's at a fairly great distance, what is the margin of error, the theoretical margin of error? Perhaps it's an abstract notion, but theoretically speaking, if we have optimal conditions, what would the margin of error be and in terms of the radius? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to explain this to you because we'd have to make an assumption. When carrying out a statistical analysis, it's a well-known fact that a series of events does not always appear in the same manner. A series of events, the mean value of deviation is called a standard deviation and 67 per cent of that standard deviation is called a possible error. Normally, 50 per cent of that dispersion, 50 per cent from that dispersion one could expect this to be a good shot, so plus or minus 50 per cent, that's 50 per cent of total dispersion. The dispersion picture in terms of percentages is between 25, 25 per cent. This is a statistical representation, in this case we're talking about dispersion. So if you fired 100 shells, 50 per cent of the shells would be in the zone plus or minus 25, plus or minus one VD, and the other 50 per cent would be the remaining six VD. So if we take six VD, we'll find 50 per cent and in the other areas, we'll find, as we're going towards the extremity of that zone, we'll find fewer and fewer shots. I hope that I have managed to explain this to a certain extent. So for example, if you are firing at 2.000 metres with 100 shells, in two VDs, according to statistics, and if the VD is accurately determined in the firing tables, you'd have 50 per cent of the shells, and outside of that zone, above or below that value, that is where you would find the other shells. So you could find shells in a range of four VDs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to make sure that I have understood something. I'm not sure that I've followed your explanation correctly when you mentioned about the -- mentioned the six remaining VDs. Could you just clarify this part of your testimony, the six remaining VDs in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If you divide the entire image into eight VDs, then the first two VDs -- you'll find 50 per cent in the first two VDs and as we move upwards, in each successive VD you will have a smaller number of shells. We take these eight segments in the first -- in the central two you'll find 50 and in the other six you'll find the other 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's clear. I would now like to focus on the so-called Markale incident. My first question, could you briefly tell us what documents you were provided with in order to carry out this analysis but, Mr. President, I would like to know how much time we have remaining so that we can plan accordingly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used a bit over three hours yesterday, as far as my computing goes and we started -- you used today 35 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I made a mistake. Yesterday, you used three and a half hours and today, you used 35 minutes, that would be a little bit over four hours whereas you have five and a half hours. We'll be very strict on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, could you answer, please?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: With the basic document to analyse and give an expert report on the Markale case was the official report of the public security station in Stari Grad and then also the report that was compiled by the expert commission of the security services centre in Sarajevo entitled the "Report on the Circumstances about the Markale Incident," and we also used a number of other documents, material. Primarily we had the UNPROFOR report about the Markale events and then we had some statements, for instance, the John Brendan Hamill, and others off the top of my head, I would have to look in my papers to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor. Professor, let me stop you here. We'll come back to that but this is because of time. Did you have the opportunity to view the videotapes that are to do with the scene at the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We also had the opportunity of viewing that and we analysed these videotapes in detail, particularly a videotape which is very interesting to assess this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, did you see a videotape, and we'll probably view this tape later on, but considering that we remember -- or we will ask you, do you remember that tape with a group of UNPROFOR soldiers and they had a French army insignia and they were handling an object in the ground, in the soil where the stabiliser may have been? Do you remember that scene; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to remember -- yes, I do remember. It's not a group of soldiers, you see just one person. On his right shoulder he's got UNPROFOR insignia with a helmet. Next to him, I think you can see a part of a face, and what's characteristic is the voice that can be heard on the videotape. I think that the voice was rather odd.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, do you remember, in particular, the soil, the view of the soil as it appears on this tape; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: On the tape, we could not see the projectile and then you can see that with a knife, there's a digging action going on, rubble is around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Our time is counted, Professor. Did you see at a certain point this image with the projectile being -- after it's been cleared, do you see the form of the projectile in the soil?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: After the rubble was taken off, it was cleared, then you can see the stabiliser -- yes, it was sometime ago that I've seen it. I think we should have a look at it again in order to be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We will. We will. But the following question: As far as your memory, what was the nature of the soil on the scene of the incident in Markale?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The soil, the ground on Markale, it seemed to be stone because there was small stones all over the place, and as far as I remember, when I compare that with the photograph, it seemed that it was a concrete cover, it seemed to have been concrete cover and that that hole was being cleared of the stones which is absolutely impossible. It cannot be accepted that a projectile had exploded there, that a mortar projectile had exploded there and that it had remained in that hole, that is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, can you please, as much as possible, answer the questions. You told me about the documents, and my following question is: How did you conduct your investigation and your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We conducted the investigation and the analysis in view of our main task which was to establish what projectile was in question and from which distance this projectile was fired. We studied the report about the circumstances of the massacre at the Markale market and we found that there were a number of omissions which would rule out certain results that were given there. First of all, one thing that is given there is that during the analysis of the angle of firing, the stabiliser was not on the scene of the incident, the stabiliser had been taken out. And by placing the stabiliser again in the hole, what was established is that the angle of descent, I think, was established being 55 to 60 per cent, I believe, 60 degrees, I believe. That is unacceptable. That is unacceptable for ascertaining the angle of descent because after the stabiliser is taken out, the error can be so great that it rules out the possibility that it is on the basis of that that we can draw a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If I may continue, first of all we ruled out this conclusion and it was -- we did not continue with this method. We wouldn't accept this value as a basis for our investigation, although we did mention this angle of descent, 55 to 60 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, now let us look at the theoretical issue of projectiles that were allegedly used. What did you -- what did you rule out? What did you establish? What can you tell us about it in terms of investigation and examination of hypothetical projectile that would have hit Markale? I'm talking about a projectile.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: All the calculations that we did as well as our long experience -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Professor Stamatovic and I have worked for over 30 years, we worked on investigating examining mortar systems. The first few years of my engineer work I myself fired a large number of these projectiles and I spent three months at -- in -- I spent three months in Bus at the specialised school and such a result that was found there, we couldn't corroborate it with any existing theory. First of all, all of the calculations and the latest method coming from the U.S. Sandia National Laboratory which works for the U.S. Army showed that it was impossible for the stabiliser of a mortar shell, 120 millimetre calibre of our performances, that is, of our drop velocities would penetrate so deeply into such a material which was given by being as Mr. Zecevic here as they said it was tarmac, that it was macadam. So we concluded on the basis of those calculations that that depth of penetration was impossible. Our starting point was to analyse the effectiveness of 120 millimetre mortar projectile. Our calculation for its effectiveness, what we took as a given was that the -- at the space of Markale, we presumed there were 1.500 people, that there were -- on the square metre turned toward the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you here, Professor. I'm going to have to stop you here. We will look at this issue a little later. We will now remain on the issue of the possibility or no possibility that the projectile, and whether this projectile could have its stabiliser penetrate into the soil. Now, on the basis of your calculations yesterday, you spoke to us about the Berezansky formula or the Berezin formula to be more precise and you said which one was the most favorable. Now, could you please clarify this and give us a precision just so there's no misunderstanding. It was -- was it stricter in terms of the defence scenario that we know or was it -- was it giving it more latitude? Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: What I said was that we took the Berezin's formula because it gave the least favorable results from the Defence's aspect because it -- more favorable results in respect of these results given in the reports of the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, to be very specific, to be very specific, if you were -- had based yourself on other formula that you mentioned, your conclusions would have been even more categorical; is this how we should understand this less favorable term that you used? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If you recall that during the testimony of the expert Zecevic, what was mentioned was the Sutterlin method, among others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to have to -- I have to interrupt you. Time is very short. Could you please answer briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If we had based our calculation only on contemporary methods used in France, which is the method used by General Sutterlin, then we would have been even more categorical in saying that it was impossible on such a soil to have such a penetration of a stabiliser under the angle that is given, 55 or 60 degrees. Some greater results would be given with a larger angle of descent, 86 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, you are moving to your next subject. Could the witness please answer your question? Your question was - and he compared it with some other systems used - the question was, to be very specific: "If you had based yourself on other formula that you mentioned, your conclusions would have been even more categorical," that's the question. That is the same question I think as whether the Berezin's formula would have been the, I would say, the most unfavorable for the Defence. That's the same question, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on this subject, we have frequently heard here testimonies in relation to a possible use of a -- the so-called time-delay fuse. If, hypothetically speaking, such a fuse, a time-delay fuse had been used on the Markale market, could the crater have appeared such as it was photographed and filmed in the documents that you received?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: No, no, it wouldn't appear like that. It would be a crater with a distinct conical surfaces with a much larger opening. At the end of the day you could have seen that in the appearance of the crater of Alipasino Polje on the 4th of February in Dobrinja. You saw that there was a crater when the projectile hit the ground. It was a large crater on such a soil, it would be narrower, it would be conical. It wouldn't be like this as it is on the ground, a hole where the stabilisers can barely fit in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, do you rule out as an expert, and I would appreciate a very brief answer, do you rule out in Markale the possibility penetration of the stabiliser in the soil and with the time-delay fuse in view of the crater that was found on the scene of the explosion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I do rule it out. If the projectile is in question, it could have only exploded on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please give us some information regarding relative velocity to do with 120 millimetre shell. What can you tell us in relation to this question, I'm speaking about the velocity of a rival initial velocity, trajectory velocity, what can you tell us very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In the firing tables that were given in the report, the excerpt, brief excerpt that was given in the report, you have the initial velocity which is V0 and the drop velocity with VC, that's how it's denoted from the first increment charge to the sixth increment charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, which table, which page?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In the English text we spoke about it yesterday on the pages where you have the main characteristics of the projectile for the 120 millimetre on page 5 of the expert analysis, you have the initial and the rival velocity of 120 millimetre shell for the maximum and minimum ranges from which you can see that the maximal drop velocity for a maximum range is 235 metres per second and for the higher range --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please speak a bit slower especially when it comes to technical terms. The translators need more time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I -- perhaps for the translators, I do understand that you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that for the lower trajectory, 235 would be the maximum drop speed and for the higher trajectory you said it would be 248 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here in the translation it says "255 millimetres." No, it's 255 metres per second and for the top charge would be 248 metres per second. Again, it says millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's clear, Professor. In relation to the quality of the surface of the soil in Markale - that's the first question - did you go to the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The location in Sarajevo was visited by Professor Stamatovic, I did not go personally, but in Markale is this site where the projectile had fallen and the situation has completely changed since so it's impossible to establish what is now truly the quality of the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you. In relation in the surface to the soil that we can imagine that it was in relation to the photos and the video that you had the opportunity of viewing, what would be the necessary velocity for a hypothetical projectile of 120 millimetres to ensure its penetration into the soil in the manner that we've examined it, that is, as deeply as we have seen it in the surface? In other terms, this velocity, would it have been possible to achieve for 120 millimetre calibre shell no matter what the distance is?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I showed you for the drop angle of 55 degrees and I provided this firing table to be copied and this related to macadam. I said that in order to penetrate the depth of 20 centimetres, for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stabiliser to penetrate to such a depth, it was necessary for the remaining velocity of the stabiliser after the pressure exerted on it caused by the explosion, I said it should be 127 metres in a second and this was in relation to a macadam surface, but if we are talking about a concrete surface then it would have to be of the order of about 600 metres. In other words, those drop velocities not such that a 120 millimetre shell can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in relation to what we viewed yesterday, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please ask the witness to indicate on the table he gave that he was just referring to where we find --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was going to be my question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about firing tables yesterday. Could you show us this table but could you also show us whether there is a table, I think it's that one there, Professor, Professor -- Professor, can you hear me? Very well. Please, concentrate on my question. I don't only want you to show us in the tables, but can you tell us where there is a table where one can read about these issues in relation to various surfaces? For example, an asphalt layer and then an earth layer or a more compact layer, this is what we are particularly interested in. These documents can now be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I showed this and I provided these tables for copying. It was a table in which the ground was either pure concrete or just a macadam surface. These tables which I also provided yesterday for you to copy, I hope you have it here, this table was compiled on the basis of the Berezin formula and the assumption made was that there was a 2 centimetre layer of concrete; in other words, that the macadam was connected with cement in the layer in order to obtain a firmer, a solid surface on which asphalt could be placed. In such a case, if the projectile falls at an angle of 55.6 degrees, and penetrates 2 centimetres of concrete, the velocity of the stabiliser has to be 44 metres. So if the drop velocity is 235 and if the rebound velocity is 144, the ejection velocity, then the difference in the velocity is the difference -- the stabiliser hits the concrete it penetrates the concrete layer of 2 centimetres and its velocity is reduced by 44 metres. The remaining velocity, so the difference between the velocity of 44 metres, it depends on whether it was -- whether it was fired with a six increment, one is left with the velocity of 81 metres. If you then use 44 metres then all you are left with in order to penetrate further is the number of 37 metres on a macadam surface. So at a velocity of 37 metres you can only penetrate a macadam surface to the depths of ten centimetres, so if you take into consideration the 2 centimetres in the concrete and the 10 centimetres, the total depth has to be less than 12 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. In other words, these tables show, if I have understood you correctly, these tables show that it's impossible to penetrate to the depth that we are familiar with; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: That's correct, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Asked and answered. I think my friend is attempting to use a document, and if he's going to use a document, may I ask that the -- this document which apparently has been created by the witness, there are some parts here in the left, the furthest left column of the document which if it is intended to be used in this Court, the counsel ought to have the witness to explain each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, is this an objection or what is at stake?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a request for the Defence to elicit from this expert an explanation of what this table exactly says, especially as far as the left column is concerned where we find A, KP times 1006 metres and then DLP and VP. That's what you are asked for to elicit from this witness for a better understanding of this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, very briefly please because we're running out of time, what does all this mean?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, the designation A is the form, the coefficient of the stabiliser form KP 10, 6 is the coefficient of the Berezansky formula for concrete, when penetrating concrete; M is the stabiliser mass, 1.2 kilograms; D is the radius -- the diameter of the stabiliser body; KP is the Berezansky coefficient for penetrating concrete; M is the stabiliser mass, 1.2 kilos; D in metres, is the diameter of the stabiliser, it's 4 centimetres; LP is penetration depth from nil nil two metres, that is to say, 2 centimetres; and VP is the necessary velocity according to the Berezansky formerly in order for the projectile to penetrate -- I apologise, for the stabiliser to penetrate concrete layer which is two centimetres thick.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. That was clear, Professor, thank you. That was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was that clear. You say KP was the factor for concrete since we find different KPs for concrete, clay, beat stone, et cetera, would it be the formula for the respective material rather than for just concrete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I have one more --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] KP is the coefficient, the value of which depends on the nature of the ground so it's nil 13 for concrete and nil 45 for macadam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say D is the diameter of the tail fin, is that in -- stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The stabiliser body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the surface, because I read somewhere else in your report that you are, I think, talking about 4 square centimetres rather than -- could we then please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D is the diameter of the stabiliser, perhaps you saw for the energy of the impact that it was joules per square centimetre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed and could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but given the time, I think that we're going to have a break now. I just want to make a comment, since there were certain interventions and questions that were put, I would just like to know how much time we have. I think it's about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very exceptional, my computing was to be preferred above the computing of Madam Registrar. You would have one hour and 24 minutes left after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps it could help if we would have the stabiliser fin nearby after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may briefly mention two matters before we proceed. The first, Mr. President, is that there was a document which the witness was referring to yesterday, a photograph, a document not in evidence, I think the Court had asked to see the originals that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that we know where it comes from and what was the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, it is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look at it at a later moment because we are still in the tables at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Secondly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Defence has brought with its expert to court a document which ought to have been part of an expert report so that it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. could have been examined before the expert testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the document you are now talking about, the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The document on the ELMO, yes, indeed, and having regard to certain matters, we may, hopefully not, but may apply that the witness be asked to remain here just for a short period so that we could complete our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you reserve your right to ask for more time for preparation for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to this issue, because the Prosecution has raised the matter, we don't have any images of the same quality that the Prosecution has. I saw that the Prosecution has seven of them, perhaps it would be useful, according to the time that we still have, to work on the basis of what the Prosecution has to place it on the ELMO and to put a few questions to the witness. It has to do with the positions on the map in the photograph, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could perhaps the original be provided to the Registry so at a suitable time that we will have a look at it and that the Defence can also have access to it in its best quality. Yes. We'll then -- Mr. Usher, would you please escort Dr. Vilicic into the courtroom again. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, following your explanations, and it's now clear to everyone, I would like you to focus on the conclusions of your colleague, Mr. Brko Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber has some question as to the table which is on the ELMO. Perhaps put it right now to the expert witness otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Vilicic, yesterday, you gave a copy already to the Chamber of a table concerning the impact velocity on the stabiliser of a mortar shell of 120 millimetres for penetration in various targets, angle of descent 55.6. It is a document which bears at the top right corner the number 5.5. Today, with the same number in the top corner, it's not visible on the ELMO, you provided us with a document which has adapted in -- has been adapted in some respect because it's -- because it now has as text added, concrete 2 centimetres over other materials, yes? When I compare these two documents, I see the following, I see that if we concentrate on the -- but let me first ask you a question: Is the whole table now about penetration in the material as indicated with a top layer of 2 centimetres of concrete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main difference between this -- these tables on the screen now and the tables that I provided you with yesterday, consists in the fact that in the table provided yesterday, the LP, the penetration depth in the first column, if we take concrete into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you? My question was whether the whole table now refers to the material indicated in the different columns and a top layer of 2 centimetres of concrete.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These tables were made in order to make it possible to make comparisons. If the concrete layer is 2 centimetres thick --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, I'm asking you a very simple question, whether the whole of the table now deals with the material indicated in the column with a surface layer of 2 centimetres concrete or that it does not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is my understanding correct that the first row of, I would say, one, two, three, four, five, six lines, so up until the first velocity P is just a 2 centimetre concrete layer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first row, yes, the velocity is 44 metres in the first column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I take you to the -- I take you to the penultimate last column, that is ground stone, could you please point at it, where it says ground stone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ground stone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point to it on the -- yes. There, you are -- the depth you are referring to is 2 centimetres, that is 0.02 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us what material you had in mind for these 2 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two centimetres, it's for ground stone, for a stabiliser to penetrate 2 centimetres of ground stone, it needs to have a velocity of 11.4 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would say that for 2 centimetres of concrete, you would need a velocity of 44 metres per second to penetrate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, this table does not directly answer what speed you would need for -- what velocity you would need to penetrate first through 2 centimetres of concrete and then to another 16 or 18 centimetres of ground stone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it doesn't provide direct information, but if you use these factors together you can come to the total depth, you can arrive at the total depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what you would need to know what velocity is required to penetrate through 2 centimetres of concrete, you'd have to take the 44 metres per second and then you would have to add the -- for every additional centimetre of ground stone the coefficient needed for ground stone as you gave it yesterday, on the previous document, where I see there's a linear function in the beat stone column saying that for 5 centimetres you would need 31.8, for 10 centimetres you would need 63.6, for 15 centimetres, you would need 95.3. So that means, for example, to come to 18 centimetres in your new assumption, that would need the 44 of the table of today for 2 centimetres of concrete, and then a little bit over --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 95.3 in order for one to reach the depth of 17 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For 17 centimetres, yes, and for each additional centimetre we would need to add approximately 6.4, 6.5 or 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now at least it is clear what this new table tells and what it does not tell us and what homework we have to do to come to the velocity required for penetrating through 2 centimetres of concrete and additional 16 centimetres of ground stone. Thank you very much for your explanation. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, there's just one matter that should be specified because I think the Professor said no in response to a question as to whether the entire table, as far as concrete is concerned, related to a layer of 2 centimetres, he said no and when I say the table itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear to me. I don't know whether it's clear to everyone. When I read the table with regard to concrete I can see in red it says concrete 2 centimetres on other materials, so it's stable for concrete, I think, but I don't know whether what the Professor said a minute ago contradicts to a slight extent these tables but if it's clear to everyone, it's clear. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's perfectly clear where in red text it says concrete 2 centimetres over other materials, then the table as such does not show the results for that situation because it is in the relevant column, it's beat stone, 2 centimetres, beat stone, 10 centimetres, beat stone and 15 centimetres and beat stone 20 centimetres, but by combining the information from the first column, which deals with 2 centimetres of concrete, together with the surface in the column on beat stone, you finally can calculate what the velocity would be needed. So if that's clear to everyone, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Professor, we'll leave these tables for a minute as well as the others and we want to turn to the conclusions of your colleague, Mr. Brko Zecevic. My first question is: Did you analyse these conclusions; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Insofar as you have analysed them, what can you tell us with regard to your own research and your own discoveries as an expert?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I have already said that -- I have already spoken of the drop angle of 55 to 65 degrees which is mentioned in the plan on the circumstances and causes of the massacre at the Markale market. And I said that that value can't be accepted and one doesn't work in this way because this was obtained on the basis of the stabiliser that was subsequently -- that subsequently penetrated that opening and then the stabiliser was probably moved, but as far as I can remember, the witness Zecevic said that he even put a device over the wings and on the basis of that, he determined the drop angle of the mine, of the shell. He used a protractor to determine this, so the drop angle is not acceptable. And furthermore, in Mr. Zecevic's testimony, several methods of calculating were mentioned, I think that it was even said that with methods that were over 150 years old, one obtained a result that it was possible for 60 metres for other velocities for the stabiliser to penetrate to a depth of 240 metres. To be precisely said, 200 to 240 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it's millimetres not metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Any other general comments?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, our conclusion was that in addition to the fact that the professional -- the material processed was professionally processed, it's not acceptable -- such a method is not acceptable given the drop angle, it's not possible for the stabiliser to penetrate in a way it was mentioned in the testimony. It was said that the 60 minus 10 metres was a sufficient velocity for the stabiliser to penetrate to that depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with regard to this expert's testimony concerning residual velocity after the shells's explosion, I'm talking the residual velocity of the body of the stabiliser, what can you tell us about the claims made by your colleague?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, they are theoretically not acceptable and practically this has not been proven. Similarly for, if my memory serves me well, for expert witness Higgs mentioned only two cases in his experience, which extends over a 20-year period, in which there are several thousand shells were fired, he only mentioned two cases in which the stabilisers penetrated the ground to such a depth. He didn't say how deep they went. He gave an example there was hard ground concerned, this was in Kenya and in Germany. He mentioned a shell which fell on a macadam road but he didn't provide any specific, any concrete information on the basis of which it would be possible to examine the matter further. He didn't say what charge was used, what distance was involved, he didn't mention the angle at which the stabilisers were found, he didn't say whether they penetrated completely or whether, as in the case of the Dobrinja incident, when shells fell on hard ground, they remained at an angle, they got stuck in the ground but they didn't penetrate. In the -- on the macadam surface as shown on that tape, it appears as if the stabiliser sunk into the macadam surface and that's totally illogical because when it explodes, everything is dispersed around the centre of the explosion. So even in the case of earth which is soft this doesn't happen, let alone in the case of macadam.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I have one question in relation to the stabiliser. If I can just deal with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was about what the findings of Dr. Zecevic on which the witness just commented were in order to see whether we talk about the same. If that will be your subject as well, please proceed if not I will like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, please do. Please. In the meantime, if I can be given the stabiliser again then we could save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, you said that, "It's not possible for the stabiliser to penetrate in a way it was mentioned in the testimony. It was said that the 60 minus 10 metres was a sufficient velocity for the stabiliser to penetrate to that depth." Is that your understanding of the testimony of Dr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. He said that it was enough for 60 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please answer my questions and the next question you're going to tell us what he said but I'd like you to read what he has said, according to the transcript. Dr. Zecevic said, and I'm referring to where he mentioned 60 and 10, he said the following: "The velocity of the shell at the time of impact is very important --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. President slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. "... which means that if the velocity of the shell is about 100 and then 60 or 70 metres per second, then the stabiliser will fall near the point of explosion. If the speed of the shell is 120, 130 metres per second, the stabilisers will fly backwards and will be 10 metres or so away. If the velocity of the shell is 200 or more metres per second, then the stabiliser will continue its trajectory and become lodged in the ground. The disruptions are short. This happens within the time frame of a microsecond." You just commented on the testimony of Dr. Zecevic being it that at a speed of 60 metre per second, the tail fin would be embedded in the ground, whereas from what I just read as the testimony of Professor Zecevic, it seems to me that what he tells us is that at 60 metres per second, the tail fin will not be embedded in the ground, and that only at a speed of some 200 metres per second then the tail fin will continue its trajectory and may be found embedded in the ground. As far as I understand his testimony, and as far as I understand your report which says that you would need the speed of over 154 metres per second in order not to be pushed back, but either to be stopped or at a higher velocity to continue its forward movement, I have some difficulties in understanding in which way your report contradicts - I'm just talking about this element - the testimony of Professor Zecevic. Could you answer to the following questions, the first one is: When you commented on the findings of Professor Zecevic, do you agree with me that what you told us his findings were does not correspond with what I just read to you as part of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the transcript of Mr. Zecevic. What you have read correctly that it's in another place; however, to the question that was asked, "Does 60 metre per second that you talk about is the velocity of penetration?" I'm reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The velocity of 60 metres per second, is it relatively small or not?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Relatively high, very high. That is his testimony in relation to the penetration of the stabiliser that 60 metres per second is a very high velocity of penetration. What has been said before is correct. Mr. Zecevic took 70 -- no, 170 metre per second as velocity of ejection and 60 metre per second added, that's 230 metre per second which is the maximum velocity that a shell in the lower end of angles would penetrate the soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first find the other quote you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have here on page 10.354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My paging is not exactly the same as you. Could you please from that part read two or three words so I can find it in my computer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous question was: [In English] "Another, we were speaking witness of the speed of penetration." Answer, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will search for the word penetration. Yes. Isn't -- I think I've found it. I think the question was, "So when you mentioned 60 metres per second, were you talking about the speed of penetration? Is it a relatively slow velocity or otherwise?" And then he said, "Relatively high." What did you understand that Dr. Zecevic meant by speed of penetration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the speed, the velocity of the stabiliser, so what he believed is that the velocity of 60 metres per second is high velocity for the penetration of stabiliser; however, the highest velocity of stabliser penetration which can be achieved during a firing on the upper end of angles, 62 degrees, is 71 metre per second. 94 metres a second if the ejection velocity is 154 metre per second which is what we went by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So 60 would be relatively high as remaining speed of penetration after the tail fin has undergone the back-pushing effect of the detonation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, under the condition that it is not linked up or related to the soil that the projectile hit. If it is related, the penetration of the stabiliser with the situation in Markale, and it is said, then 60 metres per second is very high velocity. That is what's not corresponding here, because the soil, the surface on Markale, as you have seen, demands much higher velocity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am going to stop you here. Your interpretation, therefore, is that when he answered the question whether this was a high velocity of penetration, that he was specifically referring to the soil in the Markale market and that he was not, in general terms, referring to an impact and a penetration velocity that could be produced by a 120 millimetre mortar shell. You would say it was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But generally speaking, 60 metres per second is high velocity compared to zero velocity of stabiliser, but I believe the way that Zecevic was speaking, was speaking in reference to Markale situation. About the penetration of stabliser in Markale, 60 metres per second velocity of the stabiliser is not very high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in order to penetrate the Markale soil, you would say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time you said that the maximum impact speed, penetration speed, well, let's say starting the penetration speed, would be 70 metres per second, that is the maximum speed of the tail fin upon landing minus the result of the back-pushing power of the detonation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. I don't think the interpretation is correct. What I said was the maximum velocity that the stabiliser can achieve after the ejection 154 metres, as we calculate it, could be 94 metres. In the situation, if we take that the ejection velocity 170 metres per second that the maximum would be 78 metres but the maximum impact velocity of a shell is 248 with a 66.2 degrees angle -- 86.2 degrees angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My recollection was not correct as far as the exact number was concerned. Well, did you also consider the part I just read to you when you contradicted Dr. Zecevic's findings? Did you take that into consideration as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. As I have already said in testifying on the other cases, on the basis -- from the report in terms of the specific case of Markale, in terms of the report of the Security Services Centre about the circumstances, causes of the Markale massacre, we studied carefully the testimonies of Professor Zecevic and of Mr. Higgs, and it is on the basis of that that we concluded it was on the basis of their analysis and their examination, we saw that our analysis had no reason to carry out any correction. We had already conducted our examination and our analysis. We waited for the testimonies to end, we had the materials, and after my presence here and discussing these matters with Professor Stamatovic in Vukasinovic, we decided that there was practically no -- there was no fresh material, no new moments in terms of our expert report and that we did not need to change anything, to make any corrections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to find where you do agree with Professor Zecevic. As far as I understand that from your report, and from the testimony of Professor Zecevic, that in order to penetrate into the soil, a tail fin should overcome the back-pushing power of the detonation upon impact, you calculated that you would need a speed of 154 metres per second to compensate that back-pushing power, and that therefore, you would need a velocity higher than 154 metres per second in order for the tail fin even to start with penetrating the soil on which the shell landed. Is my understanding of where you agree with Professor Zecevic correct apart from your further calculation of surfaces, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we agree except that our velocity, 154 metres per second has been calculated for our 120 millimetre shell which has been filled with TNT and this 154 figure is a difference because of the difference of these values of velocity. He said 140 to 170 and we established our value of 154 exactly for the projectile in question. That is for a shell of 120 millimetre calibre of Yugoslav manufacture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber noticed that there are slight differences in the exact data on 120 millimetre shells as far as explosives in it and the mass concerned, but thank you for these answers. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to try and summarise all this because I'm afraid I've lost you a little. You spoke on pages 42 and 43 in answering one of the questions of the Chamber that in order to begin penetrating the surface of Markale, that it should be higher velocity, you spoke of higher velocity. What is the relationship, if we can establish that of the residual velocity, what is the relationship between the -- your conclusion and the conclusion of expert Zecevic and what I mean is what is the -- mathematically speaking, mathematical relation?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I presume that in terms of mathematical relation what you mean is the values of the velocity. Do you mean the degree of velocity or do you mean the way that we have calculated this, the method of calculation?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, Professor, no. To put it more simply, you have probably found some figures. For instance, is this 50 per cent higher or 200 per cent higher? Is your difference 200 per cent? I'm speaking about the difference between your conclusion about the residual velocity on impact on blast, to be more precise, and the conclusion of expert Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, now I have understood you. Our conclusion that the stabiliser of the 120 millimetre mortar shell that is fired from a mortar with the highest possible degree of -- angle of descent could be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat -- could the witness stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
